title: The Burdah
hookLine: al-Busiri, healed after a dream of the Prophet ﷺ, writes the poem of the cloak
tomorrow: why would a family keep a poet's book right beside the Qur'an?

cards: In a hospital waiting room, people reach for whatever words they have: a verse, a song, a name to call on. Al-Busiri, a poet in Egypt, did that in verse. Tradition tells it this way.
He's struck by an illness that leaves half his body unable to move. He writes a long poem in praise of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and recites it, asking God for healing.
That night he dreams the Prophet touches him and lays his cloak over him. He wakes, and he can stand. The poem takes its name from that cloak: the Burdah.

teach.h: IT OPENS LIKE A LOVE POEM.
teach.b: It doesn't start where you'd expect. It opens like an old Arabic love poem: is it the memory of neighbors at Dhu Salam, the poet asks himself, that has your tears running mixed with blood?

teach.h: THEN THE EGO, THEN THE PRAISE.
teach.b: Then it turns on his own ego and its tricks, and only after that comes the praise: the Prophet's character, his birth, his night journey, and at the end, a plea for his intercession on the Last Day.
People sing it at gatherings in his honor and at home. And here Muslims honestly differ. One view: the Burdah is love set to verse.
The Prophet's intercession on the Last Day is in the hadith, so a line asking for it is asking him to plead with God for you; that's what reciters mean.
The other view, held by some scholars: a few lines go too far, like the one where the poet says he has no one to shelter in but the Prophet when the great calamity comes.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: REFUGE IS GOD'S ALONE.
teach.b: Refuge belongs to God alone, they say, and praise must never blur that.
Notice what both sides share: love for the Prophet, and care for the oneness of God. They disagree on where a line of poetry lands.

how: Sufi gatherings and families recite or sing the Burdah, often in the month of the Prophet's birth; some scholars who object to particular lines leave those lines out or don't recite it.

o: a poem praising the Prophet, named for a dream cloak
the white cloak a pilgrim wears on the way to Mecca
a sermon given each Friday just before the prayer

games.q: the poem of the cloak — tap the pairs.
p: tears for neighbors at Dhu Salam

s: the Burdah's critics object to praising the Prophet at all
they object to a few lines, such as taking refuge in him, which they say belongs to God alone.
the Burdah opens like an old Arabic love poem, weeping over a place
the memory of neighbors at Dhu Salam; the praise comes later.
the healing story is told inside the poem's own verses
it's the story tradition tells about how the poem came to be.

games.q: two friends: one sings the Burdah every Thursday night; the other won't. the first asks you, honestly, what the second is thinking. what's her best case?
o: she thinks any poem about the Prophet is forbidden.
she just doesn't like the tune; it's taste, not belief.
she loves the Prophet too, and wants refuge kept for God alone.
games.why: the critics' best case isn't against praise; it's care for the oneness of God. and the reciters' best case: asking for his intercession is asking him to plead with God.

practice: If you have a recording of the Burdah's opening, let it play softly through the sit, even if the Arabic is new to you. If not, listen for one sound in the room that you'd normally ignore, and follow it until it fades.

wordCard.voice: The Burdah: al-Busiri's poem in praise of the Prophet, named for the cloak he saw in a dream, sung with love and argued over with care.

orig.note: Arabic: the cloak or mantle; the name al-Busiri's poem is known by.

carryVoice: Tuck this away: the poem of the cloak, loved and debated by people who love the same Prophet. Poets, one of six.

sources.ref: al-Busiri, al-Kawakib al-Durriyya fi Madh Khayr al-Bariyya (the Burdah): opening verse (neighbors at Dhu Salam), the section on the ego, the praise, and the closing plea for intercession
the account of al-Busiri's illness and healing dream, as reported about the poem (e.g. Ibn Shakir al-Kutubi, Fawat al-Wafayat)
Sahih al-Bukhari 7510 (the Prophet's intercession on the Last Day)
